covers.quote: The same applies to adverbial and adjectival phrases and clauses.
If you don’t put the modifier in the right place, people will find it difficult to understand your content.

examples.note: The modifier clause is placed adjacent to the clause/word it clarifies, avoiding ambiguity.

parts.quote: The report suggested that the drug is beneficial, even though it’s harmful in larger doses.

examples.note: Misplaced modifier: 'Even though it's harmful in larger doses' appears adjacent to 'the report', creating ambiguity about whether 'it' refers to the report or the drug.

parts.quote: Even though it’s harmful in larger doses, the report suggested the drug is beneficial.

rules.quote: Place modifying words, such as adjectives and adverbs, next to the thing that they’re modifying.
rules.specification: Modifiers (words, phrases, or clauses) should be positioned adjacent to the word or constituent they modify to prevent unintended ambiguity or misplaced modification.
rules.violation_condition: a modifying word, phrase, or clause placed away from the element it modifies (a misplaced or squinting modifier)
when: The rule applies to modifying words as well as adverbial and adjectival phrases and clauses.
rules.why: G-2 (single rule covering words, phrases, and clauses acting as modifiers) and E-1/E-2 (matching Write this / Not this examples to the misplaced modifier rule).
